item.title: Why smart organizations miss obvious threats
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Why smart organizations miss obvious threats

Most organizational failures don't happen because leaders lack information. They happen because organizations fail to recognize what they already know.

Posted August 20, 2026

Key points
  • Organizations miss threats when they fail to recognize signals they already have.
  • Psychological safety helps people speak up, but incentives and coordination determine whether anyone acts.
  • Specialized teams often see pieces of a threat, but no one sees the whole.
  • AI can surface hidden patterns, but it cannot replace human judgment.

Why smart organizations miss obvious threats

Most organizational failures don't happen because leaders lack information. They happen because organizations fail to recognize what they already know.

Ask executives why companies get blindsided by disruption and you'll hear the same explanations.

"No one saw it coming."

"The market changed overnight."

"It was impossible to predict."

History tells a different story.

Before most disruptions become obvious, they appear as weak signals: customers behaving differently, employees raising concerns, competitors experimenting with new business models. Someone almost always sees the change coming. The challenge isn't collecting more information. It's recognizing what matters in the information the organization already possesses, before it's too late.

In Rogue Waves, I wrote that the biggest competitive advantage isn't predicting the future. It's recognizing weak signals before everyone else dismisses them as noise.

Our brains aren't wired to embrace inconvenient truths. They're wired to preserve certainty.

The cost of fitting in

Irving Janis called it groupthink: cohesive groups prioritize agreement over critical evaluation. Confirmation bias makes us seek evidence that supports what we already believe. Conformity pressures people to protect relationships instead of raising uncomfortable questions.

These aren't flaws in character. They're features of human psychology, often reinforced by hierarchy, incentives, and culture. Employees learn quickly which ideas are rewarded and which ones quietly disappear.

That's why organizations rarely fail because no one recognized the problem. They fail because the people who recognized it didn't believe the organization was ready to hear it.

The elephant problem

In the classic parable, several blind men touch different parts of an elephant. A trunk becomes a snake, a leg is a tree, and a tail becomes a rope. None are wrong; they just hold a piece of the picture.

Organizations work the same way. Sales notices changing customer expectations. Operations sees supply chain disruptions. Finance feels margin pressure. HR watches burnout climb. Marketing spots a new competitor. Each team holds a piece of the truth, but the pieces rarely come together on their own.

This is the Elephant Problem: organizations don't suffer from a lack of intelligence. They suffer because intelligence is fragmented across departments, reporting structures, and functional silos.

A 2026 study of 576 employees published in Social Behavior and Personality found something worth sitting with: psychological safety strengthened team performance, but that effect weakened as teams became more diverse in the specialized knowledge they held. Diversity of knowledge is exactly the resource an organization needs to see the whole animal.

Psychological safety turns out to be necessary, but the Elephant Problem shows it isn't sufficient on its own. Someone, or some process, still has to pull the trunk, the leg, and the tail into one description of the animal.

Weak signals are hidden in plain sight

Organizations didn’t fail during COVID-19 because the risk was unknowable, but because it was ignored. SARS, H1N1, MERS, Ebola, and years of risk assessments had already flagged them as possibilities. Prior to 2020, most of America's largest public companies did not identify pandemics as a material business risk in their annual filings.

The information existed. The significance of that information wasn't recognized until it became impossible to ignore.

That's how weak signals work. Sometimes a pattern is hard to distinguish from noise in the moment. More often it’s a well-documented risk that simply never made it onto anyone's list of things worth acting on.

Psychological safety gets you the signal, not the decision

Google’s Project Aristotle found that the strongest predictor of team performance wasn't intelligence, experience, or technical expertise. It was psychological safety. Amy Edmondson's research similarly shows that organizations learn faster when people feel safe asking difficult questions and challenging assumptions before those assumptions become expensive.

A 47-country study released in 2026 by the Center for Organizational Effectiveness found that psychological safety must be actively maintained as work pressures rise and AI reshapes roles and reporting lines.

Psychological safety lets the person holding the trunk say "I think this might be a snake" out loud, in a room full of people who are sure it's a tree. An organization that punishes dissent will never hear about the trunk at all.

But saying it out loud isn't the same as acting on it.

Psychological safety produces the raised hand, not the decision, the budget, or the authority to act on what got said. Those come from the incentives that make speaking up worth the risk, and the coordination that gets the observation to someone who can act on it. Without either one, psychological safety just produces a room full of people who feel safe saying true things that go nowhere.

Organizational debt hides reality

Even when someone raises their hand, the signal still has to travel. Every approval layer, reporting step, standing committee, and additional meeting seems reasonable on its own. Together, they create friction that slows information before it reaches the people who can act on it.

An urgent warning becomes a quarterly report. A customer complaint becomes a forgotten dashboard metric. A competitive threat becomes next year's strategic initiative, filed away until it is too late.

Reality hasn't changed. Only the organization's ability to recognize it has. It's the same Elephant Problem again, just measured in process instead of departments: every extra layer between a signal and a decision-maker is one more place a fragment of the picture can get lost.

Fixing the coordination problem

The companies adapting fastest aren't necessarily the ones investing the most in AI. They are redesigning how knowledge moves so people can act faster. Travelers, for instance, uses AI-powered knowledge management to surface expertise from across the organization, so frontline employees can decide without waiting on the management chain. Similarly, Microsoft has been experimenting with “work charts” that structure teams around shared tasks rather than strict reporting lines.

Both approaches solve the same underlying friction: they connect the pieces of the elephant before administrative layers can isolate them.

What leaders must unlearn

Safety, incentives, and coordination are all things people build. None show up automatically. Deciding what deserves attention takes judgment, and that's exactly what technology doesn't replace.

One of the most dangerous failures of judgment is quiet: if everyone agrees, we must be right. Consensus feels reassuring. Sometimes it's the first warning sign.

Organizational failure is rarely an information problem. It is an action problem. The leaders who thrive won't be the ones who predict the future best. They'll be the ones who build organizations where someone can say the elephant might be a snake, and the room stops to check.

item.title: How Can Leaders Help Support Employees’ Family Lives?
item.description:
Career

How Can Leaders Help Support Employees’ Family Lives?

Why intentional support for parents pays off for organizations and teams.

Posted August 20, 2026

Key points
  • Events like COVID-19 caused many to reflect on the balance between work and family.
  • The academic research on work-family is rich with insights on how to manage these two domains.
  • Via intentional interactions, flexibility, and professionalism, family and work can coexist.

Co-authored by Dr. Thomas Kelemen.

As we all know, the COVID-19 pandemic shifted the employee-employer relationship. Overnight, companies had to reassess policies to let workers perform their job duties from the seclusion of their homes. In many households, however, children were under stay-at-home orders. This unprecedented dynamic created palpable tension during the pandemic. Indeed, the internet was full of videos of parents juggling work alongside their children.

With the pandemic well behind us, many workers have returned to the office. But make no mistake, the trend of flexible work arrangements is here to stay, with regulations potentially on the way. However, with the transition back to the office, many managers are grappling with new expectations regarding work-family balance. Employees—especially working parents—are interested in arrangements that accommodate their personal lives, including their children or aging parents. As such, managers need to learn not only how to manage their own work-life balance but also how to manage situations in which their subordinates’ lives and work begin to overlap.

For example, with ever-changing dynamics, employees may want (or need) to occasionally bring their child to work—presenting a unique situation for a boss who may not be used to managing this type of situation. In fact, companies are increasingly offering daycare at work, and overlap between one’s “job” and “family” is often inevitable. Not surprisingly, researchers have long been interested in topics such as these. Thus, loosely based on our recent survey of the work-life literature, here are some insights that managers and human resource professionals should keep in mind as they pursue a family-friendly work environment.

Intentional Interaction

Continuing with our example of letting children come to work, there are ways in which managers can create intentional interactions. Indeed, practitioners are often encouraging organizations to embrace the practice of designated days to bring children to work, such as “Take Your Child to Work Day.” This—or other comparable days—allows children to glimpse the working day of their parents. Alternatively, employees can showcase their workspace after hours or on a Saturday for a carefree “parent-child” date.

Bringing children to work in a way that is deliberate and intentional. If done properly, these experiences can be highly impactful for children, as they carry these memories with them for the rest of their lives. For example, seeing a parent work may be the foundation of a strong work ethic or a high degree of self-efficacy that carries with the child throughout their life. Additionally, the positive impact of this type of intentional interaction aligns with academic research: studies show that organizations that adopt family-friendly policies have employees who are less likely to turn over, and family friendly policies are positively correlated with job satisfaction. Of course, there are other ways in which managers can create intentional interactions, such as back-to-school work picnics that allow people to bring their family and friends if they desire.

Be Flexible With Working Parents

Of course, managers need to be careful that life doesn’t spill over every single day at work. Yet, managers can empower employees, including letting them work from home with children. (The same logic would apply to those who have other caregiving responsibilities, such as elderly parents.) In certain cases, this flexibility may be a win for the organization as well in the long run. Research on mothers with nursing babies has shown that there can be positive outcomes associated with breastfeeding at work. Emergency situations (e.g., canceled school day or a sick babysitter) might similarly require accommodation from managers and could elicit feelings of gratitude or job satisfaction from the benefactors of this workplace flexibility. During the holiday season, spring break, or summer vacation, it is especially important that employers recognize that working parents have limited options when it comes to childcare. Regardless of the circumstances, managers should be aware that research in this space has shown a gender division: among entrepreneurs in Uganda, 37% of women brought small children to work compared to 0% of men.

Unfortunately, working parents are all-too-often discriminated against. It is a relief when people are given the benefit of the doubt, as demonstrated by a viral TikTok video of a mother who took her child to a job interview and still landed the gig. When interruptions occur, overreacting or "freezing in the moment" can often make things worse. If a child interrupts a Zoom call, mute yourself, respectfully help the child, and then promptly return to the meeting. Academic evidence suggests that this type of reaction could lead employees to be seen as more authentic, trustworthy, and human. If an employee is struggling to find a long-term solution, be a family-friendly boss and consider making a unique arrangement that considers job duties and the family member in question.

Be Professional

With all of this in mind, work is, well, work. Managers need to clearly communicate the expectations of a particular job and make sure that employees understand boundaries. Workers need to be able to get into the flow, present to clients, and have critical team meetings. Indeed, many work environments continue to place a strong emphasis on professionalism. Letting family spill over to work constantly can also undermine the ability to accomplish deep work. Further, the worksite can be dangerous, such as construction sites. As we write in the paper, “managers can be more successful in handling these situations as they…keep children safe.” Thus, it is important that managers do not comprise the integrity of the workplace, which may require situations in which reasonable boundaries on professionalism need to be put in place.

In conclusion, as the CEO of Palo Alto Software notes, it can be nearly impossible to separate work and life; these two domains can either conflict or enrich one another. Although new trends have caused us to question the work-family relationship, the need to reconcile work and family has a long history. When it comes to family and work, we encourage managers and HR professionals to integrate these three principles as a way of being a family-friendly employer: intentional interaction, flexibility, and professionalism.

Dr. Thomas Kelemen is an associate professor at Texas Tech University.

item.title: 5 Things I Learned About Breastfeeding That You Should Know
item.description:
Postpartum Depression

5 Things I Learned About Breastfeeding That You Should Know

Emerging evidence offers insights into the benefits of breastfeeding.

Posted August 20, 2026

Key points
  • Breast milk contains hormones and immune factors that change over time to support infant development.
  • Successful breastfeeding depends on accurate information and individualized support, not common myths.
  • New studies reveal connections between breastfeeding, maternal sleep, and postpartum mental health.
Source: staticnak1983/Getty Images

During Breastfeeding Awareness Month last year, I wrote about the benefits and possible difficulties associated with breastfeeding. These were the considerations that I share with my patients who are trying to make an informed decision about whether they will try breastfeeding. This year, as Breastfeeding Awareness Month approached, I looked for new studies and more information, and I was surprised to find there’s a lot more to learn.

1. Breast milk’s composition changes over 24 hours. Our energizing cortisol level peaks in the morning to help us wake up and slowly drops during the day, and then our brain’s master clock increases melatonin, which makes us sleepy at night. Breast milk levels of both therefore also change. Since very young babies don’t have fully developed circadian rhythms yet (the body’s 24-hour cycles), breast milk feeding with corresponding cortisol and melatonin levels seems to be helping them adjust to their new environment by being more alert in the morning and ready to fall asleep at night.1

2. Breast milk changes its nutritional, hormonal, and immunological components to match the nursing child's needs as they mature. Breast milk contains biologically active compounds including anti-inflammatories, antimicrobial enzymes, cytokines, immune cells, prebiotics, white blood cells, and maternal antibodies—compounds that seem to reduce the risk of some infant infections, including ear and gastrointestinal infections, while they are being breastfed.

3. Although most women who stop breastfeeding early think they aren’t producing enough milk, that’s often not the case.3 Mothers usually draw this conclusion if the baby cries frequently, feeds often, wakes a few times during the night, or seems hungry after feeding. Actually, none of these are very reliable signs of low milk supply. Pediatricians say the best way to tell if your baby is getting enough milk is to keep track of wet and dirty diapers, and your child’s weight gain. About six wet diapers a day starting with day four, and normal weight gain, are both usually signs that your milk supply is sufficient. Keep in mind, however, that the more you breastfeed on demand, the more milk you make; supplementing breast milk with formula because you are concerned about sufficient breast milk supply will usually mean that soon you really will be producing less milk. Every person is different, so check with your doctor to be sure.

4. Most of us have read that breastfeeding lowers rates of postpartum depression, but it may not be breastfeeding itself that is causing the reduction. Some factors do seem to point to a causal connection between breastfeeding and a lower risk of postpartum depression:

  • Nursing generates the release of the hormone oxytocin, which reduces stress, calms us, and promotes feelings of maternal attachment.
  • Breastfeeding lowers cortisol levels. While cortisol is good for waking up, excess cortisol can cause a fight-or-flight reaction, so lower levels help us become more even-tempered and less likely to dwell on depressing negatives.
  • Biochemical changes during nursing can lower physical inflammation, a common postpartum depression symptom.

But other explanations for this connection include:

  • Due to the amount of energy breastfeeding requires, mothers who struggle with a history of depression or anxiety (two conditions that tend to deplete energy levels) are less likely to try breastfeeding.
  • Because depression magnifies and creates physical pain as well as psychological pain, fewer mothers with depression will be able to nurse.
  • A sufficient income, strong support group, and paid leave are factors in both mental health and breastfeeding success, so these other factors could be strongly correlated with lower postpartum depression, not breastfeeding alone.
  • Successfully breastfeeding, if that was your plan, can increase your sense of control and self-esteem, and both can help fight depression.4

5. Surprisingly, breastfeeding mothers seem to get more nighttime sleep. A research review of more than seven studies that included more than 6,000 mothers found breastfeeding mothers averaged slightly more sleep than non-breastfeeding mothers. I did a deeper dive to find the reasons:

  • Breast milk is ready for a late-night feeding without taking the extra time to mix, warm, or pour into bottles.
  • Fast feeding means that mother and child are more likely to still be sleepy when it’s time to go back to bed.
  • Nursing releases prolactin and oxytocin, two hormones that calm and soothe both mother and child and make them feel relaxed and drowsy.
  • The prolactin also helps to increase the mother’s deep sleep, a phase that buffers noise and promotes rest.5,6

Formula feeding can give you and your baby closeness and bonding, but breastfeeding has special benefits for both mother and child. If it’s your choice, enjoy the experience!
